From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [List of blind musicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_blind_musicians&redirect=no "List of blind musicians"))

Visually impaired singers or instrumentalists

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/St_cecilia_guido_reni.jpg/250px-St_cecilia_guido_reni.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_cecilia_guido_reni.jpg)

_[Saint Cecilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint\_Cecilia "Saint Cecilia")_ by [Guido Reni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_Reni "Guido Reni"), 1606

[Video 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/62/Jagannath_Puriloi_Jaboloi_Ualu_Assamese_Tukari_Geet_Sung_by_Arun_Bhuyan.webm?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=job&utm_content=original)

Assamese Tukari Geet Sung by Arun Bhuyan, a blind singer from Assam

**Blind musicians** are singers or instrumentalists, or in some cases singer-accompanists, who are legally [blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blindness "Blindness").

In the past, blind musicians often had to learn on their own because formal training relied heavily on written notation. Today, tools like Braille music and large collections of accessible scores have opened up far more opportunities. Although technology has improved, many programs are still hard to use without sight, but dedicated organizations now offer strong support to help blind musicians learn, create, and grow independently.

## Resources

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Resources")]

Historically, many blind musicians, including some of the most famous, have performed without the benefit of formal instruction, since such instruction relies extensively on written musical notation. However, today there are many resources available for blind musicians who wish to learn Western [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory") and [classical notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_notation "Musical notation"). [Louis Braille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Braille "Louis Braille"), the man who created the [braille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braille "Braille") alphabet for the blind, also created a system of classical notation for the blind called [Braille music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braille_music "Braille music"). This system allows the blind to read and write music much as the sighted do. The largest collection of Braille musical scores is located at the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") in Washington, D.C.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-1) Outside the U.S., the largest collection of braille music scores is stored at the [National Library for the Blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Library_for_the_Blind "National Library for the Blind") in England.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-2)

Computer technology and the Internet make it possible in theory for blind musicians to be more independent in composing and studying music. In practice, however, most programs rely on [graphical user interfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface"), which are difficult for the blind to [navigate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigate "Navigate"). There has been some progress in creating screen-reading interfaces for the blind, especially for the [Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") operating systems.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-3)

Today there are also several organizations devoted to the support of blind musicians. The National Resource Center for Blind Musicians and The Music Education Network for the Visually Impaired are dedicated to musical education for the blind.

## Image

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Image")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Maler_der_Grabkammer_des_Nacht_001.jpg/250px-Maler_der_Grabkammer_des_Nacht_001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Maler_der_Grabkammer_des_Nacht_001.jpg)

A blind harpist, from a mural of the Eighteenth dynasty of Egypt, 15th century BC

The image of the blind musician is an important touchstone in many cultures, even where the influence of the blind on music has been limited. The idea of [Homer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer "Homer"), the blind poet, for example, has had a long existence in Western tradition, even though its basis in truth is uncertain. The legendary 6th century [Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_people "Breton people")[druid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Druidry "Druidry") and [bard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bard "Bard")[Kian Gwenc'hlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwenc'hlan "Gwenc'hlan") is depicted as being imprisoned after having his eyes gouged out for refusing to convert to Christianity and singing out that he isn't afraid to die.

In his book _[Singer of Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singer\_of\_Tales?action=edit&redlink=1 "Singer of Tales (page does not exist)")_, [Albert Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Lord "Albert Lord") explains that in [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslavia "Yugoslavia") he found many stories of blind musicians, but few current musicians who were actually blind.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-4) Natalie Kononenko had a similar experience in [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), though one Turkish musician of great talent, [Ashik Veysel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%82%C5%9F%C4%B1k_Veysel "Âşık Veysel"), was in fact blind.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-natalie-5) The popularity of the idea of the blind musician has inspired several artists. [John Singer Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Singer_Sargent "John Singer Sargent") painted a 1912 canvas based on this theme,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-6) and [Georges de La Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_de_La_Tour "Georges de La Tour") has a whole series of paintings devoted to blind musicians.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-7)

Though the idea of blind musicians may be even more prevalent than their actuality, it remains true that at many points in history and in many different cultures, blind musicians, individually or as a group, have made important contributions to the development of music. Some of these contributions are discussed below.

Blind musicians have also appeared in Muslim [harems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harem "Harem") to entertain the patron and his wives.

[Robert Heinlein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Heinlein "Robert Heinlein") made a science fiction use of the "blind bard" theme in "[The Green Hills of Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Green_Hills_of_Earth "The Green Hills of Earth")".

## Blind musicians in tradition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Blind musicians in tradition")]

### In China

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: In China")]

Further information: [Music Bureau §Music Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Bureau#Music_Masters "Music Bureau")

Court musician was a traditional profession for the blind in China in antiquity. The first musician mentioned in Chinese sources, [Shi Kuang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Bureau#Music_Masters "Music Bureau"), was a blind performer in the 6th century BC. The Guilds of Blind Musicians and Fortune-Tellers, which were still around in China during the middle of the 20th century, claimed to have existed as far back as 200 BC. More recently, groups of blind buskers have continued to perform in Zuoquan County, and presumably in other areas as well.

One of the most popular musical works in China, "[Erquan Yingyue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erquan_Yingyue?action=edit&redlink=1 "Erquan Yingyue (page does not exist)") (Moon Reflected in the Second Spring)", was composed in the first half of the 20th century by [Hua Yanjun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hua_Yanjun "Hua Yanjun"), better known as "Blind Ah Bing".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-9)

### In Japan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: In Japan")]

In Japan, [Heike Biwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heike_Biwa?action=edit&redlink=1 "Heike Biwa (page does not exist)"), a form of narrative music, was invented and spread during the [Kamakura period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamakura_period "Kamakura period") (1185–1333) by traveling musicians known as [biwa hoshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biwa_hoshi "Biwa hoshi"), who were often blind. These musicians played the [biwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biwa "Biwa"), a kind of lute, and recited stories, of which the most famous was [The Tale of the Heike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tale_of_the_Heike "The Tale of the Heike"). The musicians were sometimes known as "blind priests" because they wore robes and shaved their heads, though they were not in fact [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist "Buddhist") priests.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-10)

[Goze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goze "Goze") were similar communities of visually impaired female [shamisen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shamisen "Shamisen") and [kokyū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koky%C5%AB "Kokyū") players who travelled around the country singing songs and begging alms.

### Kobzars of Ukraine

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Kobzars of Ukraine")]

There is a long tradition of performance by blind minstrels in [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") known as _[Kobzarstvo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobzarstvo "Kobzarstvo")_. At least from 1800 to 1930 — and probably well before that as well — the majority of [itinerant](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/itinerant "wikt:itinerant") musicians in Ukraine were blind. Music was an important part of the culture. Those who could not work at other occupations could be apprenticed to become professional bards, often referred to as _[kobzars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobzar "Kobzar")_ (both [bandura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandura "Bandura") and [lira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lira_(Ukrainian_instrument) "Lira (Ukrainian instrument)") players could be referred to by this title). These wandering blind minstrels were divided into two groups—[bandurists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandurist "Bandurist"), or _[kobzars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobzar "Kobzar")_ who played [bandura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandura "Bandura"), and _[lirnyks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lirnyk "Lirnyk")_, who played the lira, which was a crank-driven [hurdy-gurdy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurdy-gurdy "Hurdy-gurdy").

The _kobzars_ were an important part of oral tradition in Ukraine. According to the ethnographer P. Zhytetsky, _kobzars_ were thought to have been initially sighted [Cossacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cossack "Cossack"), who were especially associated with [epic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_poetry "Epic poetry") songs, or _[dumas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duma\_(epic) "Duma (epic)")_. Kononenko states that _lirnyks_, on the other hand, were blind church singers organized into guilds who sang religious songs and were often associated with [beggars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beggars "Beggars"). By the middle of the 19th century, the two groups had merged; both sang many different types of songs, all were organized into the guilds, and all were blind.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/%D0%92%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9E%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BF_%D0%B7_%D0%B4%D1%80%D1%83%D0%B6%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BE%D1%8E.jpg/250px-%D0%92%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9E%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BF_%D0%B7_%D0%B4%D1%80%D1%83%D0%B6%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BE%D1%8E.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%92%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9E%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BF_%D0%B7_%D0%B4%D1%80%D1%83%D0%B6%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BE%D1%8E.jpg)

[Ostap Veresai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostap_Veresai "Ostap Veresai"), the most famous _kobzar_ of the 19th century, with his wife. Like the other _kobzars_ of his day, Veresai was blind.

The _kobzars_ have a central place in the national identity of Ukraine. Folklorist [Izmail Sreznevskyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izmail_Sreznevskyi "Izmail Sreznevskyi") argued that the initial [Cossack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cossack "Cossack")[bandurists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandurist "Bandurist") were actual witnesses of the great battles about which they sang. The image of warrior-bards singing [epics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_epic "National epic") was quite popular, and there became a tradition that the great ancient singers were veterans valorously blinded in combat. This in turn led to the belief that the kobzar tradition had greatly weakened in the 19th century, since the traditional songs were now sung by people who were more like beggars than like warriors. Kononenko points out that there is no factual basis for this image, and her research showed that the minstrel tradition was still very strong and creative up until the 1930s.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-natalie-5)

Because the art of the _kobzars_ was language-specific and included themes dealing with historic subjects of Ukraine's past, the blind singers were often the focus of persecution by occupying powers, according to researcher [Mikhailo Khay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhailo_Khay?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mikhailo Khay (page does not exist)"). This persecution reached its height under [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin") in the 1930s, when many forms of Ukrainian cultural expression were crushed by the communist government of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). In the late 1930s many bandurists were arrested and some shot. Documents have been discovered to show that the renowned bandurist [Hnat Khotkevych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hnat_Khotkevych "Hnat Khotkevych") was executed in 1938 and the blind _kobzar_[Ivan Kucherenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Kucherenko "Ivan Kucherenko") was shot in 1937.

Numerous sources claim that there was an organized large scale massacre of Ukrainian blind musicians in the 1930s, though this has not been confirmed by official documents, and most details of the incident (including year, place, and method of execution) are disputed. Traditional blind minstrelsy by the late 1930s had largely vanished.

Today, the traditional repertoire of the _kobzars_ is performed by sighted, educated performers. During her research in Ukraine, Kononenko found only one blind folk performer of the old songs, a man named [Pavlo Suprun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavlo_Suprun?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pavlo Suprun (page does not exist)"), who had studied bandura playing and voice at the Kiev State Conservatory.

### Traditional Irish musicians

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Traditional Irish musicians")]

During the medieval and early modern eras, [harpists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpist "Harpist"), [pipers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipe_(instrument) "Pipe (instrument)"), and other musicians traveled around Ireland, providing music for dances and other occasions. As in Ukraine, many of the Irish musicians were blind. It was common practice for blind or disabled children to be taught a musical instrument as a means of supporting themselves, as they could not perform hard labour.

The most famous of these blind musicians, harper [Turlough O'Carolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O_Carolan "O Carolan"), composed many tunes that have become part of the traditional repertoire, including "Sidh Beag Sidh Mór" and "Carolan's Concerto".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-11)

Others included [Eoghain Ó Cianáin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eoghain_%C3%93_Cian%C3%A1in "Eoghain Ó Cianáin") (fl. 1540), [Nicholas Dáll Pierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_D%C3%A1ll_Pierce "Nicholas Dáll Pierce") (fl. 1601), [William fitz Robert Barry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_fitz_Robert_Barry "William fitz Robert Barry") (fl. 1615), [Ruaidri Dáll Ó Catháin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruaidri_D%C3%A1ll_%C3%93_Cath%C3%A1in "Ruaidri Dáll Ó Catháin") (died 1653), [Higgins of Tyrawley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgins_of_Tyrawley "Higgins of Tyrawley") (fl. 18th century), and [Martin O'Reilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_O'Reilly "Martin O'Reilly") (1829–1904).

### Blind organists in Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Blind organists in Europe")]

There is a long tradition of blind organists, including Louis Braille himself. In the 20th century some of the greatest organists were blind, including the great German Bach scholar and teacher [Helmut Walcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Walcha "Helmut Walcha") (1907–1991), and a number of prominent French organists and composers for the organ including [Louis Vierne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Vierne "Louis Vierne") (1870–1937), [Andre Marchal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andre_Marchal "Andre Marchal") (1894–1980), [Gabriel Gauthier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Gauthier "Gabriel Gauthier") (1808-1853), [Gaston Litaize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaston_Litaize "Gaston Litaize") (1909–1991), and [Jean Langlais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Langlais "Jean Langlais") (1907–1991), as well as one of the current organists at [Notre Dame de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre_Dame_de_Paris "Notre Dame de Paris"), [Jean-Pierre Leguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Leguay "Jean-Pierre Leguay") (b. 1939). England has also produced brilliant blind organists in the 18th, 19th and 20th centuries, including [John Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stanley_(composer) "John Stanley (composer)") (1712-1786), [John Purkis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Purkis "John Purkis") (1781-1849), [George Warne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Warne_(organist) "George Warne (organist)") (1792-1868), [William Wolstenholme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wolstenholme "William Wolstenholme") (1865-1931), [Alfred Hollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hollins "Alfred Hollins") (1865-1942) and David A. Liddle (b. 1960), the latter a student of Marchal and who currently enjoys an international performing career. Yet it is a tradition which goes back even further: to 14th-century Italian [Francesco Landini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Landini "Francesco Landini") (?–1397) and Spanish baroque master [Antonio de Cabezon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_de_Cabezon "Antonio de Cabezon") (1510–1566). One could argue that even [Johann Sebastian Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach") and [George Frederic Handel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Frederic_Handel "George Frederic Handel"), who lost their sight late in life but presumably continued to play and compose, should be included in this discussion, along with the great American popular organist [George Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wright_(organist) "George Wright (organist)") (1920–1998), who likewise lost his sight late in life but continued to present concerts and make sound recordings until his death. Blind composer [Frances McCollin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_McCollin "Frances McCollin") (1892–1960) won the Clemson Prize from the [American Guild of Organists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Guild_of_Organists "American Guild of Organists") in 1918. She studied organ with another blind musician, [David Duffield Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Duffield_Wood "David Duffield Wood") (1838–1910), the organist at Philadelphia's St. Stephen's Episcopal Church for many years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-DiMedio-12)

### Blind piano tuners

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Blind piano tuners")]

In 19th century France and England, piano tuners were frequently blind. The first blind [piano tuner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_tuner "Piano tuner") is thought to be [Claude Montal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Montal "Claude Montal"), who taught himself how to tune a piano while studying at [L'Institut National des Jeunes Aveugles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Institution_for_Blind_Youth "Royal Institution for Blind Youth") in 1830. At first Montal's teachers were skeptical, doubting that a blind man could actually perform the necessary mechanical tasks. Montal's skill was undeniable, however, and he was soon asked to teach classes in tuning to his fellow students. Eventually, he also overcame public [prejudice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prejudice "Prejudice"), and landed several prestigious jobs as a tuner for professors and professional musicians. Montal's success paved the way for other blind tuners, both in France and in England, where Montal's example and teaching methods were adopted by [Thomas Rhodes Armitage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Armitage "Thomas Armitage"). Today the image of the blind piano tuner is so ingrained that people in England sometimes express surprise when they encounter a piano tuner who can see.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-13) An organization of blind piano tuners remains active in Britain.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-14)

### American country blues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: American country blues")]

Blind musicians have made a significant contribution to American popular music. This is particularly true in [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music"), [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), and other predominantly African American forms – perhaps because discrimination at the time made it more difficult for black blind people to find other employment.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In any case, the achievement of blind African-Americans in music is extensive. The first recorded gospel [sanctified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctification "Sanctification")[barrelhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juke_joint "Juke joint") piano player, [Arizona Dranes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_Dranes "Arizona Dranes"), was blind, as were [Al Hibbler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Hibbler "Al Hibbler"), and [Ray Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Charles "Ray Charles"), one of the most important figures in the creation of [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"). [Art Tatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Tatum "Art Tatum"), commonly cited as the greatest jazz pianist of all time, was also almost blind. [Stevie Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Wonder "Stevie Wonder"), who is blind from birth, has recorded more than thirty U.S. top ten hits and won twenty-two Grammy Awards[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-15) (the most ever won by a solo artist in history).

However, blind black musicians are still most strongly associated with the [country blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_blues "Country blues"). The first successful male country blues performer, [Blind Lemon Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Lemon_Jefferson "Blind Lemon Jefferson"), was blind, as were many other country bluesmen, including [Blind Willie McTell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Willie_McTell "Blind Willie McTell"), [Blind Willie Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Willie_Johnson "Blind Willie Johnson"), [Sonny Terry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Terry "Sonny Terry"), [Blind Boy Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Boy_Fuller "Blind Boy Fuller"), [Blind Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Blake "Blind Blake") and [Reverend Gary Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverend_Gary_Davis "Reverend Gary Davis"). The figure of the blind country bluesman became so iconic that when [Eddie Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Lang "Eddie Lang"), a sighted jazz guitarist, wanted to choose a black pseudonym for purposes of recording blues records with [Lonnie Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonnie_Johnson_(musician) "Lonnie Johnson (musician)"), he naturally settled on [Blind Willie Dunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Willie_Dunn "Blind Willie Dunn").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-16)[Bogus Ben Covington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogus_Ben_Covington "Bogus Ben Covington") was known for pretending to be blind. [John William Boone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_William_Boone "John William Boone"), known as "Blind Boone", was an important American pianist and composer of ragtime.

## Modern blind musicians

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Modern blind musicians")]

[Ronnie Milsap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Milsap "Ronnie Milsap") is an American singer, songwriter, and musician. He began his career as a [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R&B "R&B") and soul artist, but is most known for his country and pop music career. [Jeff Healey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Healey "Jeff Healey") was a blind Juno Award-winning and Grammy Award-nominated Canadian blues-rock vocalist and guitarist, who attained musical and personal popularity, particularly in the 1980s and 1990s. The American guitarist and songwriter, [Doc Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Watson "Doc Watson"), was blinded before his first birthday from an eye infection, and went on to become an influential musician in American bluegrass and folk music, known for his proficient flatpicking and fingerpicking skills on guitar as well as his extensive knowledge of traditional American songs.

The Italian pop [tenor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor "Tenor"), [Andrea Bocelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Bocelli "Andrea Bocelli"), who was born with congenital [glaucoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucoma "Glaucoma") and completely lost his sight at the age of 12, after a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") accident,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-People1998-17) is the biggest-selling singer in the history of classical music,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-21) with worldwide sales exceeding [70 million copies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_music_artists#50_million_to_74_million_records "List of best-selling music artists")[_[broken anchor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOS:BROKENSECTIONLINKS "MOS:BROKENSECTIONLINKS")_].[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-Forbes_2016-05-10-22)

In 2009, Japanese [Nobuyuki Tsujii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobuyuki_Tsujii "Nobuyuki Tsujii"), at age 20, became the first blind pianist to win the top prize at a major international competition, the 13th [Van Cliburn International Piano Competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Cliburn_International_Piano_Competition "Van Cliburn International Piano Competition"). He was also awarded the Beverley Taylor Smith Award for the Best Performance of a New Work. He played all twelve of [Frédéric Chopin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Chopin "Frédéric Chopin")'s [Op. 10 Études](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tudes_(Chopin) "Études (Chopin)") as part of his performance in the preliminaries. Born blind, Tsujii developed his own technique for learning complex classical piano works.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-23) With videos of his piano performances widely viewable on the Internet, Tsujii's competition win has made him an international sensation. As of 2010, Tsujii's discography includes ten CDs, some of which have sold over 100,000 copies.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-24) As a Van Cliburn winner, Tsujii has been performing in concerts all over the world.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-25)

One of the prominent blind South Indian [carnatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnatic_music "Carnatic music") musicians is [M. Chandrasekaran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._Chandrasekaran "M. Chandrasekaran"), a violin maestro who has received some of the highest awards by many musical institutions in India. His musical career spans over six decades and he has travelled to perform in many music festivals all over India and the world.

[Ravindra Jain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravindra_Jain "Ravindra Jain") (28 February 1944 – 9 October 2015) was an Indian blind-born music composer, lyricist and playback singer. He started his career in the early 1970s, composing for hit movies such as _Chor Machaye Shor_ (1974), _Geet Gaata Chal_ (1975), _Chitchor_ (1976) and _Ankhiyon Ke Jharokhon Se_ (1978). He composed music for many films and TV shows based on Hindu epics, including Ramanand Sagar's _Ramayan_ (1987). He was awarded the Padma Shri, the fourth-highest civilian award of the Republic of India in 2015 for his contribution to the arts.

**Blind musicians** are singers or instrumentalists, or in some cases singer-accompanists, who are legally [blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blindness "Blindness").

In the past, blind musicians often had to learn on their own because formal training relied heavily on written notation. Today, tools like Braille music and large collections of accessible scores have opened up far more opportunities. Although technology has improved, many programs are still hard to use without sight, but dedicated organizations now offer strong support to help blind musicians learn, create, and grow independently.

## Resources

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Resources")]

Historically, many blind musicians, including some of the most famous, have performed without the benefit of formal instruction, since such instruction relies extensively on written musical notation. However, today there are many resources available for blind musicians who wish to learn Western [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory") and [classical notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_notation "Musical notation"). [Louis Braille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Braille "Louis Braille"), the man who created the [braille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braille "Braille") alphabet for the blind, also created a system of classical notation for the blind called [Braille music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braille_music "Braille music"). This system allows the blind to read and write music much as the sighted do. The largest collection of Braille musical scores is located at the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") in Washington, D.C.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-1) Outside the U.S., the largest collection of braille music scores is stored at the [National Library for the Blind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Library_for_the_Blind "National Library for the Blind") in England.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-2)

Computer technology and the Internet make it possible in theory for blind musicians to be more independent in composing and studying music. In practice, however, most programs rely on [graphical user interfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphical_user_interface "Graphical user interface"), which are difficult for the blind to [navigate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigate "Navigate"). There has been some progress in creating screen-reading interfaces for the blind, especially for the [Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows "Microsoft Windows") operating systems.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-3)

Today there are also several organizations devoted to the support of blind musicians. The National Resource Center for Blind Musicians and The Music Education Network for the Visually Impaired are dedicated to musical education for the blind.

## Image

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Image")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Maler_der_Grabkammer_des_Nacht_001.jpg/250px-Maler_der_Grabkammer_des_Nacht_001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Maler_der_Grabkammer_des_Nacht_001.jpg)

A blind harpist, from a mural of the Eighteenth dynasty of Egypt, 15th century BC

The image of the blind musician is an important touchstone in many cultures, even where the influence of the blind on music has been limited. The idea of [Homer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer "Homer"), the blind poet, for example, has had a long existence in Western tradition, even though its basis in truth is uncertain. The legendary 6th century [Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breton_people "Breton people")[druid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Druidry "Druidry") and [bard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bard "Bard")[Kian Gwenc'hlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwenc'hlan "Gwenc'hlan") is depicted as being imprisoned after having his eyes gouged out for refusing to convert to Christianity and singing out that he isn't afraid to die.

In his book _[Singer of Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singer\_of\_Tales?action=edit&redlink=1 "Singer of Tales (page does not exist)")_, [Albert Lord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Lord "Albert Lord") explains that in [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslavia "Yugoslavia") he found many stories of blind musicians, but few current musicians who were actually blind.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-4) Natalie Kononenko had a similar experience in [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), though one Turkish musician of great talent, [Ashik Veysel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%82%C5%9F%C4%B1k_Veysel "Âşık Veysel"), was in fact blind.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-natalie-5) The popularity of the idea of the blind musician has inspired several artists. [John Singer Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Singer_Sargent "John Singer Sargent") painted a 1912 canvas based on this theme,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-6) and [Georges de La Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_de_La_Tour "Georges de La Tour") has a whole series of paintings devoted to blind musicians.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-7)

Though the idea of blind musicians may be even more prevalent than their actuality, it remains true that at many points in history and in many different cultures, blind musicians, individually or as a group, have made important contributions to the development of music. Some of these contributions are discussed below.

Blind musicians have also appeared in Muslim [harems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harem "Harem") to entertain the patron and his wives.

[Robert Heinlein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Heinlein "Robert Heinlein") made a science fiction use of the "blind bard" theme in "[The Green Hills of Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Green_Hills_of_Earth "The Green Hills of Earth")".

## Blind musicians in tradition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Blind musicians in tradition")]

### In China

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: In China")]

Further information: [Music Bureau §Music Masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Bureau#Music_Masters "Music Bureau")

Court musician was a traditional profession for the blind in China in antiquity. The first musician mentioned in Chinese sources, [Shi Kuang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Bureau#Music_Masters "Music Bureau"), was a blind performer in the 6th century BC. The Guilds of Blind Musicians and Fortune-Tellers, which were still around in China during the middle of the 20th century, claimed to have existed as far back as 200 BC. More recently, groups of blind buskers have continued to perform in Zuoquan County, and presumably in other areas as well.

One of the most popular musical works in China, "[Erquan Yingyue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erquan_Yingyue?action=edit&redlink=1 "Erquan Yingyue (page does not exist)") (Moon Reflected in the Second Spring)", was composed in the first half of the 20th century by [Hua Yanjun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hua_Yanjun "Hua Yanjun"), better known as "Blind Ah Bing".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-9)

### In Japan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: In Japan")]

In Japan, [Heike Biwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heike_Biwa?action=edit&redlink=1 "Heike Biwa (page does not exist)"), a form of narrative music, was invented and spread during the [Kamakura period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamakura_period "Kamakura period") (1185–1333) by traveling musicians known as [biwa hoshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biwa_hoshi "Biwa hoshi"), who were often blind. These musicians played the [biwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biwa "Biwa"), a kind of lute, and recited stories, of which the most famous was [The Tale of the Heike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tale_of_the_Heike "The Tale of the Heike"). The musicians were sometimes known as "blind priests" because they wore robes and shaved their heads, though they were not in fact [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist "Buddhist") priests.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-10)

[Goze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goze "Goze") were similar communities of visually impaired female [shamisen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shamisen "Shamisen") and [kokyū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koky%C5%AB "Kokyū") players who travelled around the country singing songs and begging alms.

### Kobzars of Ukraine

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Kobzars of Ukraine")]

There is a long tradition of performance by blind minstrels in [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") known as _[Kobzarstvo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobzarstvo "Kobzarstvo")_. At least from 1800 to 1930 — and probably well before that as well — the majority of [itinerant](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/itinerant "wikt:itinerant") musicians in Ukraine were blind. Music was an important part of the culture. Those who could not work at other occupations could be apprenticed to become professional bards, often referred to as _[kobzars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobzar "Kobzar")_ (both [bandura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandura "Bandura") and [lira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lira_(Ukrainian_instrument) "Lira (Ukrainian instrument)") players could be referred to by this title). These wandering blind minstrels were divided into two groups—[bandurists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandurist "Bandurist"), or _[kobzars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobzar "Kobzar")_ who played [bandura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandura "Bandura"), and _[lirnyks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lirnyk "Lirnyk")_, who played the lira, which was a crank-driven [hurdy-gurdy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurdy-gurdy "Hurdy-gurdy").

The _kobzars_ were an important part of oral tradition in Ukraine. According to the ethnographer P. Zhytetsky, _kobzars_ were thought to have been initially sighted [Cossacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cossack "Cossack"), who were especially associated with [epic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_poetry "Epic poetry") songs, or _[dumas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duma\_(epic) "Duma (epic)")_. Kononenko states that _lirnyks_, on the other hand, were blind church singers organized into guilds who sang religious songs and were often associated with [beggars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beggars "Beggars"). By the middle of the 19th century, the two groups had merged; both sang many different types of songs, all were organized into the guilds, and all were blind.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/%D0%92%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9E%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BF_%D0%B7_%D0%B4%D1%80%D1%83%D0%B6%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BE%D1%8E.jpg/250px-%D0%92%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9E%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BF_%D0%B7_%D0%B4%D1%80%D1%83%D0%B6%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BE%D1%8E.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%92%D0%B5%D1%80%D0%B5%D1%81%D0%B0%D0%B9_%D0%9E%D1%81%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BF_%D0%B7_%D0%B4%D1%80%D1%83%D0%B6%D0%B8%D0%BD%D0%BE%D1%8E.jpg)

[Ostap Veresai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostap_Veresai "Ostap Veresai"), the most famous _kobzar_ of the 19th century, with his wife. Like the other _kobzars_ of his day, Veresai was blind.

The _kobzars_ have a central place in the national identity of Ukraine. Folklorist [Izmail Sreznevskyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izmail_Sreznevskyi "Izmail Sreznevskyi") argued that the initial [Cossack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cossack "Cossack")[bandurists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandurist "Bandurist") were actual witnesses of the great battles about which they sang. The image of warrior-bards singing [epics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_epic "National epic") was quite popular, and there became a tradition that the great ancient singers were veterans valorously blinded in combat. This in turn led to the belief that the kobzar tradition had greatly weakened in the 19th century, since the traditional songs were now sung by people who were more like beggars than like warriors. Kononenko points out that there is no factual basis for this image, and her research showed that the minstrel tradition was still very strong and creative up until the 1930s.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-natalie-5)

Because the art of the _kobzars_ was language-specific and included themes dealing with historic subjects of Ukraine's past, the blind singers were often the focus of persecution by occupying powers, according to researcher [Mikhailo Khay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhailo_Khay?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mikhailo Khay (page does not exist)"). This persecution reached its height under [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin") in the 1930s, when many forms of Ukrainian cultural expression were crushed by the communist government of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"). In the late 1930s many bandurists were arrested and some shot. Documents have been discovered to show that the renowned bandurist [Hnat Khotkevych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hnat_Khotkevych "Hnat Khotkevych") was executed in 1938 and the blind _kobzar_[Ivan Kucherenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Kucherenko "Ivan Kucherenko") was shot in 1937.

Numerous sources claim that there was an organized large scale massacre of Ukrainian blind musicians in the 1930s, though this has not been confirmed by official documents, and most details of the incident (including year, place, and method of execution) are disputed. Traditional blind minstrelsy by the late 1930s had largely vanished.

Today, the traditional repertoire of the _kobzars_ is performed by sighted, educated performers. During her research in Ukraine, Kononenko found only one blind folk performer of the old songs, a man named [Pavlo Suprun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavlo_Suprun?action=edit&redlink=1 "Pavlo Suprun (page does not exist)"), who had studied bandura playing and voice at the Kiev State Conservatory.

### Traditional Irish musicians

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Traditional Irish musicians")]

During the medieval and early modern eras, [harpists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpist "Harpist"), [pipers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipe_(instrument) "Pipe (instrument)"), and other musicians traveled around Ireland, providing music for dances and other occasions. As in Ukraine, many of the Irish musicians were blind. It was common practice for blind or disabled children to be taught a musical instrument as a means of supporting themselves, as they could not perform hard labour.

The most famous of these blind musicians, harper [Turlough O'Carolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O_Carolan "O Carolan"), composed many tunes that have become part of the traditional repertoire, including "Sidh Beag Sidh Mór" and "Carolan's Concerto".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-11)

Others included [Eoghain Ó Cianáin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eoghain_%C3%93_Cian%C3%A1in "Eoghain Ó Cianáin") (fl. 1540), [Nicholas Dáll Pierce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_D%C3%A1ll_Pierce "Nicholas Dáll Pierce") (fl. 1601), [William fitz Robert Barry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_fitz_Robert_Barry "William fitz Robert Barry") (fl. 1615), [Ruaidri Dáll Ó Catháin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruaidri_D%C3%A1ll_%C3%93_Cath%C3%A1in "Ruaidri Dáll Ó Catháin") (died 1653), [Higgins of Tyrawley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgins_of_Tyrawley "Higgins of Tyrawley") (fl. 18th century), and [Martin O'Reilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_O'Reilly "Martin O'Reilly") (1829–1904).

### Blind organists in Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Blind organists in Europe")]

There is a long tradition of blind organists, including Louis Braille himself. In the 20th century some of the greatest organists were blind, including the great German Bach scholar and teacher [Helmut Walcha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helmut_Walcha "Helmut Walcha") (1907–1991), and a number of prominent French organists and composers for the organ including [Louis Vierne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Vierne "Louis Vierne") (1870–1937), [Andre Marchal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andre_Marchal "Andre Marchal") (1894–1980), [Gabriel Gauthier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Gauthier "Gabriel Gauthier") (1808-1853), [Gaston Litaize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaston_Litaize "Gaston Litaize") (1909–1991), and [Jean Langlais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Langlais "Jean Langlais") (1907–1991), as well as one of the current organists at [Notre Dame de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre_Dame_de_Paris "Notre Dame de Paris"), [Jean-Pierre Leguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Pierre_Leguay "Jean-Pierre Leguay") (b. 1939). England has also produced brilliant blind organists in the 18th, 19th and 20th centuries, including [John Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stanley_(composer) "John Stanley (composer)") (1712-1786), [John Purkis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Purkis "John Purkis") (1781-1849), [George Warne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Warne_(organist) "George Warne (organist)") (1792-1868), [William Wolstenholme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wolstenholme "William Wolstenholme") (1865-1931), [Alfred Hollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hollins "Alfred Hollins") (1865-1942) and David A. Liddle (b. 1960), the latter a student of Marchal and who currently enjoys an international performing career. Yet it is a tradition which goes back even further: to 14th-century Italian [Francesco Landini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Landini "Francesco Landini") (?–1397) and Spanish baroque master [Antonio de Cabezon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_de_Cabezon "Antonio de Cabezon") (1510–1566). One could argue that even [Johann Sebastian Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach") and [George Frederic Handel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Frederic_Handel "George Frederic Handel"), who lost their sight late in life but presumably continued to play and compose, should be included in this discussion, along with the great American popular organist [George Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wright_(organist) "George Wright (organist)") (1920–1998), who likewise lost his sight late in life but continued to present concerts and make sound recordings until his death. Blind composer [Frances McCollin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frances_McCollin "Frances McCollin") (1892–1960) won the Clemson Prize from the [American Guild of Organists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Guild_of_Organists "American Guild of Organists") in 1918. She studied organ with another blind musician, [David Duffield Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Duffield_Wood "David Duffield Wood") (1838–1910), the organist at Philadelphia's St. Stephen's Episcopal Church for many years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-DiMedio-12)

### Blind piano tuners

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Blind piano tuners")]

In 19th century France and England, piano tuners were frequently blind. The first blind [piano tuner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_tuner "Piano tuner") is thought to be [Claude Montal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Montal "Claude Montal"), who taught himself how to tune a piano while studying at [L'Institut National des Jeunes Aveugles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Institution_for_Blind_Youth "Royal Institution for Blind Youth") in 1830. At first Montal's teachers were skeptical, doubting that a blind man could actually perform the necessary mechanical tasks. Montal's skill was undeniable, however, and he was soon asked to teach classes in tuning to his fellow students. Eventually, he also overcame public [prejudice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prejudice "Prejudice"), and landed several prestigious jobs as a tuner for professors and professional musicians. Montal's success paved the way for other blind tuners, both in France and in England, where Montal's example and teaching methods were adopted by [Thomas Rhodes Armitage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Armitage "Thomas Armitage"). Today the image of the blind piano tuner is so ingrained that people in England sometimes express surprise when they encounter a piano tuner who can see.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-13) An organization of blind piano tuners remains active in Britain.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-14)

### American country blues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: American country blues")]

Blind musicians have made a significant contribution to American popular music. This is particularly true in [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), [gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_music "Gospel music"), [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), and other predominantly African American forms – perhaps because discrimination at the time made it more difficult for black blind people to find other employment.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In any case, the achievement of blind African-Americans in music is extensive. The first recorded gospel [sanctified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctification "Sanctification")[barrelhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juke_joint "Juke joint") piano player, [Arizona Dranes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_Dranes "Arizona Dranes"), was blind, as were [Al Hibbler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Hibbler "Al Hibbler"), and [Ray Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Charles "Ray Charles"), one of the most important figures in the creation of [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music"). [Art Tatum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Tatum "Art Tatum"), commonly cited as the greatest jazz pianist of all time, was also almost blind. [Stevie Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Wonder "Stevie Wonder"), who is blind from birth, has recorded more than thirty U.S. top ten hits and won twenty-two Grammy Awards[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-15) (the most ever won by a solo artist in history).

However, blind black musicians are still most strongly associated with the [country blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_blues "Country blues"). The first successful male country blues performer, [Blind Lemon Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Lemon_Jefferson "Blind Lemon Jefferson"), was blind, as were many other country bluesmen, including [Blind Willie McTell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Willie_McTell "Blind Willie McTell"), [Blind Willie Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Willie_Johnson "Blind Willie Johnson"), [Sonny Terry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Terry "Sonny Terry"), [Blind Boy Fuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Boy_Fuller "Blind Boy Fuller"), [Blind Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Blake "Blind Blake") and [Reverend Gary Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverend_Gary_Davis "Reverend Gary Davis"). The figure of the blind country bluesman became so iconic that when [Eddie Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Lang "Eddie Lang"), a sighted jazz guitarist, wanted to choose a black pseudonym for purposes of recording blues records with [Lonnie Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonnie_Johnson_(musician) "Lonnie Johnson (musician)"), he naturally settled on [Blind Willie Dunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_Willie_Dunn "Blind Willie Dunn").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-16)[Bogus Ben Covington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogus_Ben_Covington "Bogus Ben Covington") was known for pretending to be blind. [John William Boone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_William_Boone "John William Boone"), known as "Blind Boone", was an important American pianist and composer of ragtime.

## Modern blind musicians

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blind_musicians&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Modern blind musicians")]

[Ronnie Milsap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_Milsap "Ronnie Milsap") is an American singer, songwriter, and musician. He began his career as a [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R&B "R&B") and soul artist, but is most known for his country and pop music career. [Jeff Healey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Healey "Jeff Healey") was a blind Juno Award-winning and Grammy Award-nominated Canadian blues-rock vocalist and guitarist, who attained musical and personal popularity, particularly in the 1980s and 1990s. The American guitarist and songwriter, [Doc Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Watson "Doc Watson"), was blinded before his first birthday from an eye infection, and went on to become an influential musician in American bluegrass and folk music, known for his proficient flatpicking and fingerpicking skills on guitar as well as his extensive knowledge of traditional American songs.

The Italian pop [tenor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor "Tenor"), [Andrea Bocelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Bocelli "Andrea Bocelli"), who was born with congenital [glaucoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucoma "Glaucoma") and completely lost his sight at the age of 12, after a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") accident,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-People1998-17) is the biggest-selling singer in the history of classical music,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-21) with worldwide sales exceeding [70 million copies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_best-selling_music_artists#50_million_to_74_million_records "List of best-selling music artists")[_[broken anchor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOS:BROKENSECTIONLINKS "MOS:BROKENSECTIONLINKS")_].[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-Forbes_2016-05-10-22)

In 2009, Japanese [Nobuyuki Tsujii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobuyuki_Tsujii "Nobuyuki Tsujii"), at age 20, became the first blind pianist to win the top prize at a major international competition, the 13th [Van Cliburn International Piano Competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Cliburn_International_Piano_Competition "Van Cliburn International Piano Competition"). He was also awarded the Beverley Taylor Smith Award for the Best Performance of a New Work. He played all twelve of [Frédéric Chopin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Chopin "Frédéric Chopin")'s [Op. 10 Études](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tudes_(Chopin) "Études (Chopin)") as part of his performance in the preliminaries. Born blind, Tsujii developed his own technique for learning complex classical piano works.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-23) With videos of his piano performances widely viewable on the Internet, Tsujii's competition win has made him an international sensation. As of 2010, Tsujii's discography includes ten CDs, some of which have sold over 100,000 copies.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-24) As a Van Cliburn winner, Tsujii has been performing in concerts all over the world.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_blind_musicians#cite_note-25)

One of the prominent blind South Indian [carnatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnatic_music "Carnatic music") musicians is [M. Chandrasekaran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._Chandrasekaran "M. Chandrasekaran"), a violin maestro who has received some of the highest awards by many musical institutions in India. His musical career spans over six decades and he has travelled to perform in many music festivals all over India and the world.

[Ravindra Jain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravindra_Jain "Ravindra Jain") (28 February 1944 – 9 October 2015) was an Indian blind-born music composer, lyricist and playback singer. He started his career in the early 1970s, composing for hit movies such as _Chor Machaye Shor_ (1974), _Geet Gaata Chal_ (1975), _Chitchor_ (1976) and _Ankhiyon Ke Jharokhon Se_ (1978). He composed music for many films and TV shows based on Hindu epics, including Ramanand Sagar's _Ramayan_ (1987). He was awarded the Padma Shri, the fourth-highest civilian award of the Republic of India in 2015 for his contribution to the arts.

_**Speak Now**_ is the third studio album by the American singer-songwriter Taylor Swift. It was released on October 25, 2010, through [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records"). Swift wrote the album entirely herself while [touring in 2009–2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_Tour "Fearless Tour") to reflect on her transition from adolescence to adulthood.

Swift framed _Speak Now_ as a loose [concept album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album") about the unsaid things she wanted to deliver to the subjects of her songs. Using confessional songwriting, the album is mostly about heartbreak and reflections on broken relationships, and some tracks were inspired by Swift's rising stardom in the public eye to address her critics and adversaries. She and [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_(record_producer) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)") produced _Speak Now_, which combines [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop"), [country rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_rock "Country rock"), [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock"), and [power pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_pop "Power pop"). Its songs incorporate prominent [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") stylings, and their melodies are characterized by acoustic instruments intertwined with chiming [electric guitars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar"), dynamic drums, and [orchestral strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_section "String section").

After the album's release, Swift embarked on the [Speak Now World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_World_Tour "Speak Now World Tour") from February 2011 to March 2012. The album was supported by six [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music) "Single (music)"), including the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") top-ten singles "[Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mine_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Mine (Taylor Swift song)")" and "[Back to December](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_December "Back to December")", and the US [Hot Country Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs") number ones "[Sparks Fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparks_Fly_(song) "Sparks Fly (song)")" and "[Ours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ours_(song) "Ours (song)")". _Speak Now_ peaked atop the charts and received [multi-platinum certifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_music_recording_certifications "List of music recording certifications") in Australia, Canada, and New Zealand. In the United States, it sold one million copies within its first week, spent six weeks at number one on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), and was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") six-times platinum for surpassing six million [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit") by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America").

Music critics generally praised _Speak Now_ for its radio-friendly melodies and emotional engagement. Some critics thought the lyrics represented Swift's maturity in early adulthood, but several others criticized the confrontational tracks as shallow. At the [54th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "54th Annual Grammy Awards") in 2012, _Speak Now_ was nominated for [Best Country Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Country_Album "Best Country Album"), and its single "[Mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_(song) "Mean (song)")" won [Best Country Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Country_Song "Best Country Song") and [Best Country Solo Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Country_Solo_Performance "Best Country Solo Performance"). The album appeared in 2010s decade-end lists by _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_ and _[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin\_(magazine) "Spin (magazine)")_, and _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ ranked it in their lists "The 50 Greatest Female Albums of All Time" (2012) and "The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far" (2025). Following the [2019 dispute regarding the ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute") of Swift's back catalog, she released the [re-recorded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recorded "Re-recorded") album _[Speak Now (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak\_Now\_(Taylor's\_Version) "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)")_ in 2023, and the [master recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_recording "Master recording") ownership of _Speak Now_ was acquired by Swift in 2025.

Me")", performed well on both [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_radio "Country radio") and [pop radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_radio "Pop radio") and brought Swift to mainstream prominence.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-4) "Love Story" was the first country song to reach number one on the [Pop Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_Songs "Pop Songs") chart and "You Belong with Me" was the first country song to top the all-genre [Radio Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Songs_(chart) "Radio Songs (chart)") chart.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-6) At the [52nd Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "52nd Annual Grammy Awards") in February 2010, _Fearless_ won [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year") and [Best Country Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Country_Album "Best Country Album"), and its single "[White Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Horse_(Taylor_Swift_song) "White Horse (Taylor Swift song)")" won [Best Female Country Vocal Country Song").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-7)

The success of _Fearless_ made Swift one of country music's biggest stars to [crossover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossover_music "Crossover music") into the mainstream market.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-billboard_best-9) At the [2009 MTV Video Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_MTV_Video_Music_Awards "2009 MTV Video Music Awards"), where Swift won [Best Female Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Female_Video "Best Female Video") for "You Belong with Me", the rapper [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West") interrupted her acceptance speech; the incident received widespread media coverage and became known as "[Kanyegate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanyegate "Kanyegate")".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-11) At the 52nd Annual Grammy Awards, Swift sang "You Belong with Me" and "[Rhiannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhiannon_(song) "Rhiannon (song)")" with [Stevie Nicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Nicks "Stevie Nicks"); ## Writing and lyrics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Speak_Now&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writing and lyrics")]

Because of her extensive touring schedule, Swift wrote her third album alone: "I'd get my best ideas at 3:00 a.m. in Arkansas, and I didn't have a co-writer around so I would just finish it. That would happen again in New York and then again in Boston and that would happen again in Nashville."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-universe-15) Inspired by her growth into adulthood, she conceived _Speak Now_ as a loose [concept album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album") about the things she wanted to tell certain people she had met but never had a chance to.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-universe-15) As with her songwriting on previous albums, Swift strove to convey emotional honesty with details as specifically as possible, believing it is important for a songwriter to do so.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-universe-15) She described her songs as "diary entries" about her emotions that helped her navigate adulthood.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-ew_songwriting-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-wsj_int-17) Swift chose not to follow the trend of making increasingly sexualized music by artists of her age and believed such a path would be incongruent with her artistic vision.[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(album)#cite_note-19)
