_Speak Now_ features a [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") sound with prominent mainstream music elements, a style that had characterized _Taylor Swift_ and _Fearless_, and is typified by the lead single and opening track, "Mine";[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-AllMusic-45)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-mcall-44)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-American_Songwriter-46)_[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_'s James Lachno described the sound as "country bubblegum-pop".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-47) The songs' arrangements are similar to those in Swift's first two albums, but the instruments' textures are more dense and evoke strong pop and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") influences.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTENainby2024100-48) According to the [musicologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musicologist "Musicologist") James E. Perone, the rock textures of _Speak Now_ are derived from 1970s and 1980s styles such as [new wave rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_rock "New wave rock") and [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201729,_42-49) There were disagreements over the album's genre classification,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-EW-50) with critics categorizing it as [country rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_rock "Country rock"),[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-American_Songwriter-46)[pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock"),[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bbc_music-51) and [power pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_pop "Power pop").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Now-52) The music critic [Ann Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Powers "Ann Powers"), in a review for the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_, described the album's sound as an extension of country-pop towards [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock") and bubblegum pop, with its tracks incorporating styles from "lush strings of [Céline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celine_Dion "Celine Dion")-style [kitsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitsch "Kitsch")-pop to Americana banjo to [countrypolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countrypolitan "Countrypolitan") electric guitar".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-LAT-20)

The [song structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_structure "Song structure") feature climatic build-ups, catchy pop melodies, and memorable [hooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_(music) "Hook (music)"),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Paste-53)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33) characterized by chiming guitars, dynamic drums, and powerful choruses.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-54) The banjo-led [bluegrass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluegrass_music "Bluegrass music") track "Mean" is the only song that critics regarded as purely country music.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-billboard_best-9)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-american_songwriter-28)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-55) "Sparks Fly" has an arena-rock and pop-rock production with guitars and subtle fiddles,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-56)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202454-57) and "Speak Now" is an acoustic guitar-driven pop song with a [1950s rock chorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'50s_progression "'50s progression").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-mcall-44)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-58) "The Story of Us" and "Better than Revenge" are electric-guitar-driven [pop-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-punk "Pop-punk") songs;[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-nytimes_review-59) the former contains influences of arena rock, [dance-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance-pop "Dance-pop"), and [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"), instrumented by electric guitar riffs and subdued [mandolin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandolin "Mandolin");[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Paste-53)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Voice-60)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202463-61) and the latter features soaring electric guitars and distorted vocals, evoking 1980s [hard rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock "Hard rock") but with more melodic accessibility.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201737Zaleski202467-62) The arena-rock and [goth-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goth-rock "Goth-rock") number "Haunted" incorporates a dramatic recurring string section.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-pitchfork-31)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-nytimes_review-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-vulture_best-63) The closing track "Long Live" is a [heartland rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heartland_rock "Heartland rock") song featuring [girl-group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girl-group "Girl-group")[harmonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_harmony "Vocal harmony") and chiming rock guitars.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-pitchfork-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-RS-32)

The remaining tracks of _Speak Now_ are [ballads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad"). "Back to December" is a gentle, orchestral, string-laden [power ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-la_times_int-26)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202456-64) "Dear John" is a slow-burning, [bluesy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), country-pop song with electric guitar [licks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lick_(music) "Lick (music)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-billboard_best-9)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Spin-65) The guitar ballad "Never Grow Up" incorporates an understated production that accompanies its wistful lyrics.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-pitchfork-31)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-mcall-44) On "Enchanted", the acoustic guitar [crescendos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crescendo "Crescendo") after each refrain and leads up to a harmony-layered [coda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coda_(music) "Coda (music)") at the end.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-pitchfork-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33) "Innocent" and "Last Kiss" incorporate sparse instruments; the latter is a slow-tempo [waltz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waltz "Waltz") with breathy vocals.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-mcall-44)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-vulture_best-63) "[If This Was a Movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/If_This_Was_a_Movie "If This Was a Movie")", a bonus song on the deluxe edition and the only song not written solely by Swift,[[note 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-67) is a fast-paced ballad with a recurring guitar [riff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff") and simple harmonies.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-68)

## Release and promotion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Speak_Now&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Release and promotion")]

Swift announced _Speak Now_ on July 20, 2010, in a [live stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_stream "Live stream") on [Ustream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ustream "Ustream").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bb_release-38) Big Machine Records released the lead single "Mine" to US [country radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_radio "Country radio") and digital download sites on August 4, 2010.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-69) The single peaked at number three on the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100")[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-70) and was certified [triple platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-71) It reached number six in Japan,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-72) number seven in Canada,[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-canadian_hot_100-73) and number nine in Australia.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-74) On August 18, Swift released the album's cover art, which depicts Swift with curly hair and red lipstick [twirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twirling "Twirling") in a deep-purple gown.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-75) On September 15, she announced a [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation "Target Corporation")-exclusive deluxe edition; the deluxe edition cover features a red gown in place of the purple gown on the standard edition cover.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-deluxe-76) Starting from October 4, 2010, Big Machine released one _Speak Now_ track each week on the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store") as part of a three-week countdown campaign; "Speak Now" was released on October 5, followed by "Back to December" on October 12 and "Mean" on October 19.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-mtv_rolling-77) On October 22, [Xfinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xfinity "Xfinity") premiered a preview of "The Story of Us".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-mtv_rolling-77)

Big Machine released the standard and deluxe editions of _Speak Now_ on October 25, 2010.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-deluxe-76)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-78) The Target-exclusive deluxe edition contains 14 songs of the standard; the bonus tracks "[Ours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ours_(song) "Ours (song)")", "If This Was a Movie", and "Superman"; acoustic versions of "Back to December" and "Haunted"; a "pop mix" of "Mine"; a 30-minute behind-the-scenes video for "Mine"; and the music video for "Mine".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-deluxe_notes-42)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-79) The deluxe edition was released to other retailers on January 17, 2012.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-80)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-81) To bolster sales of the album, Swift had partnerships with [Starbucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starbucks "Starbucks"), [Sony Electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Electronics "Sony Electronics"), [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart "Walmart"), and [Jakks Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakks_Pacific "Jakks Pacific").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-promo_tour-82)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bb_marketing-83) In October 2011, Swift partnered with [Elizabeth Arden, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Arden,_Inc. "Elizabeth Arden, Inc.") to release her fragrance brand "Wonderstruck", whose name references the lyrics of "Enchanted".[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bb_marketing-83)

To further promote _Speak Now_, Swift appeared on magazine covers and conducted press interviews.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ew_songwriting-16) She performed "Innocent" at the [2010 MTV Video Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_MTV_Video_Music_Awards "2010 MTV Video Music Awards").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-84) Her other performances at awards shows include the [Country Music Association Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Country_Music_Association_Awards "2010 Country Music Association Awards")[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-85) and the [American Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Music_Awards_of_2010 "American Music Awards of 2010") in 2010;[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-86) the [Academy of Country Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Country_Music_Awards "Academy of Country Music Awards")[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-87) and the [Country Music Association Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Country_Music_Association_Awards "2011 Country Music Association Awards") in 2011.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-88) She also performed at a benefit concert for the [Country Music Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_Music_Hall_of_Fame "Country Music Hall of Fame"), held at [Club Nokia L.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L.A._Live "L.A. Live")[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-89) In Europe, Swift performed on [BBC Radio 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_2 "BBC Radio 2") and _[X Factor Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X\_Factor\_(Italian\_TV\_series) "X Factor (Italian TV series)")_, and she had interviews with [BBC Radio 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_1 "BBC Radio 1") in the United Kingdom and [NRJ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRJ "NRJ") in France.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-solid-90) She embarked on a promotional tour in Japan, where she appeared on the television shows _[SMAPxSMAP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMAPxSMAP "SMAPxSMAP")_ and _[Music Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music\_Station "Music Station")_.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Billboard/Schwartz-91) Her round of American television shows included _[Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Today\_(U.S.\_TV\_program) "Today (U.S. TV program)")_, _[Late Show with David Letterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late\_Show\_with\_David\_Letterman "Late Show with David Letterman")_, _[The Ellen DeGeneres Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ellen\_DeGeneres\_Show "The Ellen DeGeneres Show")_, _[Live with Regis and Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_with\_Regis\_and\_Kelly "Live with Regis and Kelly")_, and _[Dancing with the Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing\_with\_the\_Stars "Dancing with the Stars")_.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-promo_tour-82) She also gave private concerts to contest winners and played a semi-private concert for [JetBlue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JetBlue "JetBlue") at the [John F. Kennedy International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport "John F. Kennedy International Airport") in New York.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-nytimes_sales-92)

After "Mine", Swift released five more singles from _Speak Now_. "Back to December" and "Mean" were released to US country radio on November 15, 2010,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-93) and March 7, 2011.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-94) The two singles peaked at numbers seven and ten in Canada,[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-canadian_hot_100-73) and "Back to December" reached number six on the _Billboard_ Hot 100.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-95) "The Story of Us" was released to US [pop radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_radio "Pop radio") on April 19, 2011.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-96) "Sparks Fly" and "Ours" were released to US country radio on July 18[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-97) and December 5, 2011.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-98) Prior to its single release, "Ours", together with the other deluxe edition tracks, was released for digital download via the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store") on November 8, 2011.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-99) "Sparks Fly" and "Ours" reached the top 20 on the _Billboard_ Hot 100 and peaked atop the [Hot Country Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs") chart.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-100)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-101) The RIAA certified all six of the album's singles at least platinum; "Back to December" and "Mean" sold over two million copies each, and they were certified double-platinum and triple-platinum.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-102)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-103)

On November 23, 2010, Swift announced the [Speak Now World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_World_Tour "Speak Now World Tour"), which started in Singapore on February 9, 2011. The tour visited Asia and Europe before the North American leg started in [Omaha, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaha,_Nebraska "Omaha, Nebraska"), on May 27, 2011.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-104) Within two days of announcement, the tour sold 625,000 tickets.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-speak_now_tops-105) By April 2011, Swift had added another 16 shows to the North American leg.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-106) After the final US concert in New York City on November 22, 2011, the Speak Now World Tour had covered 80 sold-out North American shows.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-107) On August 10, 2011, Swift released a music video for "Sparks Fly" that includes footage from the tour.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-108) She released the album _[Speak Now World Tour– Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak\_Now\_World\_Tour\_%E2%80%93\_Live "Speak Now World Tour – Live")_ on November 21, 2011.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-109) In December 2011, Swift announced an extension of the tour to Australia and New Zealand starting in March 2012.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-110) Concluding on March 18, 2012, the Speak Now World Tour had covered 110 shows, visited 18 countries,[[note 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-112) and grossed $123.7 million.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-tour_recap-111)

## Commercial performance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Speak_Now&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Commercial performance")]

Before _Speak Now_'s release, Big Machine shipped two million copies of the album to stores in the United States.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-reuters-29) In the week ending November 13, 2010, the album debuted at number one on the _Billboard_ 200 chart, with first-week sales of 1,047,000 copies.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bb_sales-113) It marked the highest single-week tally for a female country artist and became the first album since [Lil Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Wayne "Lil Wayne")'s _[Tha Carter III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tha\_Carter\_III "Tha Carter III")_ (2008) to sell over one million copies in its first week of release.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-114) Media publications including _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_,[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bb_sales-113)[MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV"),[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-promo_tour-82) and _The New York Times_[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-nytimes_sales-92) published articles highlighting _Speak Now_'s strong sales in the context of declining [record sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_sales "Record sales") brought about by the emergence of [music download](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_download "Music download") platforms. According to _The New York Times_, although the music industry in 2010 saw album sales "[plunging] by more than 50 percent in the last decade", the album proved Swift "has transcended the limitations of genre and become a pop megastar".[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-nytimes_sales-92) The _[Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness\_World\_Records "Guinness World Records")_ in 2010 recognized _Speak Now_ as the fastest-selling album in the United States by a female country artist.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-115)

In _Speak Now_'s first charting week, 11 of the standard edition's 14 tracks charted on the _Billboard_ Hot 100, making Swift the first female artist to have 11 songs on the Hot 100 at the same time.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-116) After the digital release of the deluxe edition tracks in November 2011, "If This Was a Movie" charted at number 10 on the Hot 100, making Swift the first artist to have eight songs debut in the top 10.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-117)[[note 6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-119) With this achievement, _Speak Now_ had four songs peaking in the top 10 of the _Billboard_ Hot 100—"Mine", "Back to December", "Speak Now", and "If This Was a Movie".[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-120) The album spent six non-consecutive weeks atop the _Billboard_ 200.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-121)_Speak Now_ was the third-best-selling album of 2010 in the United States with sales of 2.96 million copies.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-122) By January 2024, it had sold 4.817 million copies in the United States.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-US2024sales-123) The RIAA [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") the album [six-times platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification"), which denotes six million [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit") based on sales, song downloads, and [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming "Streaming").[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-RIAA-124)

_Speak Now_ was a chart success in the wider English-speaking world: it peaked atop the albums charts of Australia,[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-aus-125) Canada,[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-126) and New Zealand,[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-new_zealand-127) and peaked at number six in Ireland[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ire-128) and the United Kingdom.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-uk_albums-129) The album was certified triple-platinum in Australia,[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-aria-130) Canada,[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-music_canada-131) and New Zealand.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-RMNZ-132) Upon conclusion of the Asian leg of the Speak Now World Tour by February 2011, the album sold 400,000 copies in the region and received platinum sales certifications in Taiwan, South Korea, Indonesia, and the Philippines.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-AsiaCerts-133) In Europe, it charted at number four in Norway and number ten in Spain.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-norway-134)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-spain-135) After Swift embarked on [the Eras Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eras_Tour "The Eras Tour") (2023–2024), _Speak Now_ resurged in popularity in the United Kingdom: it re-entered the top 40 (at number 23) on the [albums chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Albums_Chart "UK Albums Chart") for the week ending May 18, 2023, which was its first top-40 appearance since November 2010.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-136)

Initial reviews of _Speak Now_ were generally positive.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-speak_now_tops-105) On the review aggregator site [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), which assigns a [normalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score "Standard score") rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, the album has an average score of 77 that was based on 20 reviews.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Speak_Now_2010:_Reviews-138) AnyDecentMusic? compiled 10 reviews and gave it an average score of 6.9 out of 10.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ADM-137)

Most reviews praised Swift's songwriting for showcasing a mature perspective on love and relationships.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-speak_now_tops-105) Reviews from [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"),[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-AllMusic-45)_Entertainment Weekly_,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-EW-50)_[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_,[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Guardian-140) the _Los Angeles Times_,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-LAT-20) and _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-RS-32) complimented the songs for portraying emotions with engaging narratives and vivid details. In AllMusic's review, [Stephen Thomas Erlewine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Thomas_Erlewine "Stephen Thomas Erlewine") wrote: "[Swift] writes from the perspective of the moment yet has the skill of a songwriter beyond her years."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-AllMusic-45)_[American Songwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American\_Songwriter "American Songwriter")_ approved of Swift's self-penned material and artistic control.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-american_songwriter-28) In his consumer guide, [Robert Christgau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Christgau "Robert Christgau") commented that although the album was too long and the romantic themes did not interest him, the songs were fascinating because of an "effort that bears a remarkable resemblance to care—that is, to caring in the best, broadest, and most emotional sense".[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Christgau-141)

The album's dramatic themes of heartbreak and vengeance received mixed reviews. _[Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Now\_(newspaper) "Now (newspaper)")_ said although it included some memorable tracks, _Speak Now_ was blemished by celebrity, rage, and grievances.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Now-52)_[Slant Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slant\_Magazine "Slant Magazine")_ lauded Swift's melodic songwriting for offering radio-friendly pop hooks but criticized the lyrics of "Dear John", "Mean", "Innocent", and "Better than Revenge" as shallow and shortsighted.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33) Meanwhile, _[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin\_(magazine) "Spin (magazine)")_ opined that the "bubblier" tracks like "Sparks Fly" and "Long Live" were forgettable, while the songs about vengeance like "Mean" and "Better than Revenge" were memorable because they explored "something nervy and intense when she goes nasty".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Spin-65) In congruence, [Steven Hyden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Hyden "Steven Hyden") from _[The A.V. Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_A.V.\_Club "The A.V. Club")_ wrote of those tracks: "Swift's niftiest trick is being at her most likeable when she's indulging in such overt nastiness."[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Hyden-139)_Entertainment Weekly_ agreed, deeming those tracks inevitable for Swift's artistic evolution.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-EW-50)_[The Village Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Village\_Voice "The Village Voice")_ said Swift's songwriting was "not confessional, but dramatic" and found it more nuanced and mature compared to that of _Fearless_.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Voice-60)

Other reviews focused on _Speak Now_'s production. Reviews published in _Paste_[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Paste-53) and _Slant Magazine_[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33) called it a catchy album with radio-friendly pop tunes; the former was impressed by the crossover appeal but deemed the overall production dull. _The Village Voice_ took issue with Swift's vocals as weak and strained.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Voice-60) BBC Music found the album's track list too long but called it overall a "sparky and affecting record".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bbc_music-51)_Now_ approved of Swift's experimentation with styles other than country but considered it "too safe" and said the album was tarnished by "slickly produced power pop and a sugary sameness [that is] indiscernible from any number of today's radio-oriented artists".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Now-52) Ann Powers appreciated _Speak Now_'s soft, introspective tracks for personalizing pop music.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-LAT-20)[Jon Caramanica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Caramanica "Jon Caramanica") of _The New York Times_ lauded the experimentation with genres such as blues and pop punk, and he called _Speak Now_ a bold step for Swift.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-nytimes_review-59)

## Accolades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Speak_Now&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Accolades")]

On year-end lists of the best albums of 2010, _Speak Now_ was ranked 12th by _American Songwriter_ and 13th by _Rolling Stone_.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-142)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-143)_The New York Times_' Jon Caramanica ranked the album number two (behind [Rick Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Ross "Rick Ross")'s _[Teflon Don](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teflon\_Don\_(album) "Teflon Don (album)")_) in his 2010 year-end list.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-144) The album appeared on lists of the best country albums of 2010; _[PopMatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PopMatters "PopMatters")_ ranked it fifth[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-145) and _[The Boot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Boot\_(website) "The Boot (website)")_ ranked it second.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-146) In 2012, _Speak Now_ appeared at number 45 on _Rolling Stone_'s list of "The 50 Greatest Female Albums of All Time"; [Rob Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Sheffield "Rob Sheffield") commented: "She might get played on the country station, but she's one of the few genuine rock stars we've got these days, with a flawless ear for what makes a song click."[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-147)

In 2019, _Billboard_ listed _Speak Now_ in 51st place on its list of the best albums of the 2010s[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-148) and second on its list of best country albums of the same decade.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-149) The album also ranked 37th on _Spin_'s 2010s decade-end list[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-150) and 71st on that of [Cleveland.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland.com "Cleveland.com");[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-151) and _[Taste of Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste\_of\_Country "Taste of Country")_ named it the fourth-best country album of the 2010s.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-152)_Rolling Stone_ placed it at number 196 on their 2025 list of "The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far", deeming it the "peak of her Nashville era".[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-153)

## Impact

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Speak_Now&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Impact")]

See also: [_Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(Taylor's_Version) "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)")

Swift has said that she wrote _Speak Now_ by herself as a reaction to critics' doubts about her songwriting ability.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-163) While reviews had emphasized the importance of co-writers on her past albums, _Speak Now_ granted Swift the definite credentials to assert authorship over her music and career.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcNutt202077Grandchamp202496-164) Some academics have upheld how the album solidified her artistry with its nuanced observations, confessional and confrontational songs about grappling with young adulthood and fame;[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201742McNutt202077-165) many retrospective reviews have considered it a groundwork to her consistent songcraft of later albums.[[note 7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-169) Its commercial success contributed to her fame as a pop star transcending her self-identity as a country-music artist.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown2012177-170)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-171)_[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork\_(website) "Pitchfork (website)")_'s Sam Sodomsky, reviewing the album in 2019, contended that her country-music identity served as an indicator of her autobiographical songwriting rather than musical style.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-pitchfork-31)

Several critics reflected on _Speak Now_ in the context of Swift's celebrity. Many of its songs were inspired by experiences that were routinely documented in the press, such as short-lived romantic relationships and the 2009 MTV Awards incident. This set a precedent to not only the confessional songwriting on Swift's later albums, but also the media speculation on the subjects behind her lyrics.[[note 8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-175)[Maura Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maura_Johnston "Maura Johnston") opined that these songs laid the groundwork to her 2017 album _[Reputation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reputation\_(album) "Reputation (album)")_, which focused on her image and confrontation against critics.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Johnston-172) According to the gender studies professor Adriane Brown, the songs about idealized romance and her innocent, "good-girl" image made her stand out in a contemporary pool of sexualized female pop artists. Brown commented that Swift's unwillingness to openly discuss sex and tendency to criticize females who "whore themselves out", as in the lyrics of "Better than Revenge", was problematic.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrown2012176%E2%80%93177-176)

In November 2020, after a [dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute") over the ownership of the [masters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastering_(audio) "Mastering (audio)") to her back catalog, Swift began [re-recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recording_(music) "Re-recording (music)") her first six studio albums.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-177) On May 5, 2023, at the first Eras Tour show in Nashville, Swift announced the re-recorded version of _Speak Now_—_[Speak Now (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak\_Now\_(Taylor's\_Version) "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)")_, and its release date on July 7.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-178)_Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ consists of re-recordings of all fourteen songs from the standard edition, the deluxe tracks "Ours" and "Superman",[[note 9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-180) and six previously unreleased "From the Vault" songs.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-181) After _Speak Now (Taylor's Version)_ was released, the original album reached new peaks in Switzerland (number one),[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-swiss-182) Austria (number one),[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-aut-183) Germany (number two),[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-germany-184) and it was certified gold in the latter two countries.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ifpi-austria-185)[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bvmi-186) The ownership of the original album's master recording, alongside her other five albums released under Big Machine, was acquired by Swift on May 30, 2025.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-187)

_**Speak Now**_ is the third studio album by the American singer-songwriter Taylor Swift. It was released on October 25, 2010, through [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records"). Swift wrote the album entirely herself while [touring in 2009–2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_Tour "Fearless Tour") to reflect on her transition from adolescence to adulthood.

Swift framed _Speak Now_ as a loose [concept album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album") about the unsaid things she wanted to deliver to the subjects of her songs. Using confessional songwriting, the album is mostly about heartbreak and reflections on broken relationships, and some tracks were inspired by Swift's rising stardom in the public eye to address her critics and adversaries. She and [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_(record_producer) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)") produced _Speak Now_, which combines [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop"), [country rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_rock "Country rock"), [pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock"), and [power pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_pop "Power pop"). Its songs incorporate prominent [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") stylings, and their melodies are characterized by acoustic instruments intertwined with chiming [electric guitars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_guitar "Electric guitar"), dynamic drums, and [orchestral strings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_section "String section").

After the album's release, Swift embarked on the [Speak Now World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_World_Tour "Speak Now World Tour") from February 2011 to March 2012. The album was supported by six [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music) "Single (music)"), including the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") top-ten singles "[Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mine_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Mine (Taylor Swift song)")" and "[Back to December](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_December "Back to December")", and the US [Hot Country Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs "Hot Country Songs") number ones "[Sparks Fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparks_Fly_(song) "Sparks Fly (song)")" and "[Ours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ours_(song) "Ours (song)")". _Speak Now_ peaked atop the charts and received [multi-platinum certifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_music_recording_certifications "List of music recording certifications") in Australia, Canada, and New Zealand. In the United States, it sold one million copies within its first week, spent six weeks at number one on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), and was [certified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RIAA_certification "RIAA certification") six-times platinum for surpassing six million [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit") by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America").

Music critics generally praised _Speak Now_ for its radio-friendly melodies and emotional engagement. Some critics thought the lyrics represented Swift's maturity in early adulthood, but several others criticized the confrontational tracks as shallow. At the [54th Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/54th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "54th Annual Grammy Awards") in 2012, _Speak Now_ was nominated for [Best Country Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Country_Album "Best Country Album"), and its single "[Mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_(song) "Mean (song)")" won [Best Country Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Country_Song "Best Country Song") and [Best Country Solo Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Country_Solo_Performance "Best Country Solo Performance"). The album appeared in 2010s decade-end lists by _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")_ and _[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin\_(magazine) "Spin (magazine)")_, and _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ ranked it in their lists "The 50 Greatest Female Albums of All Time" (2012) and "The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far" (2025). Following the [2019 dispute regarding the ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_masters_dispute "Taylor Swift masters dispute") of Swift's back catalog, she released the [re-recorded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-recorded "Re-recorded") album _[Speak Now (Taylor's Version)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak\_Now\_(Taylor's\_Version) "Speak Now (Taylor's Version)")_ in 2023, and the [master recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_recording "Master recording") ownership of _Speak Now_ was acquired by Swift in 2025.

Taylor Swift released hеr second studio album _[Fearless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless\_(Taylor\_Swift\_album) "Fearless (Taylor Swift album)")_ through [Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville "Nashville")-based [Big Machine Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Machine_Records "Big Machine Records") in November 2008. music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_music "Country music") artist.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-2) It was the best-selling album of 2009 in the United States, making then-20-year-old Swift the youngest artist to have an annual best-seller since [Nielsen SoundScan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_SoundScan "Nielsen SoundScan") began tracking album sales in 1991.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-3) Two of the album's [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music) "Single (music)"), "[Love Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Story_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Love Story (Taylor Swift song)")" and "[You Belong with Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Belong_with_Me "You Belong with Me")", performed well on both [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_radio "Country radio") and [pop radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_radio "Pop radio") and brought Swift to mainstream prominence.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-4) "Love Story" was the first country song to reach number one on the [Pop Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_Songs "Pop Songs") chart and "You Belong with Me" was the first country song to top the all-genre [Radio Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Songs_(chart) "Radio Songs (chart)") chart.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-6) At the [52nd Annual Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/52nd_Annual_Grammy_Awards "52nd Annual Grammy Awards") in February 2010, _Fearless_ won [Album of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Album_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Album of the Year") and [Best Country Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Country_Album "Best Country Album"), and its single "[White Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Horse_(Taylor_Swift_song) "White Horse (Taylor Swift song)")" won [Best Female Country Vocal Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Female_Country_Vocal_Performance "Best Female Country Vocal Performance") and [Best Country Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Country_Song "Best Country Song").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-7)

The success of _Fearless_ made Swift one of country music's biggest stars to [crossover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossover_music "Crossover music") into the mainstream market.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-billboard_best-9) At the [2009 MTV Video Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_MTV_Video_Music_Awards "2009 MTV Video Music Awards"), where Swift won [Best Female Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Female_Video "Best Female Video") for "You Belong with Me", the rapper [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West") interrupted her acceptance speech; the incident received widespread media coverage and became known as "[Kanyegate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanyegate "Kanyegate")".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-11) At the 52nd Annual Grammy Awards, Swift sang "You Belong with Me" and "[Rhiannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhiannon_(song) "Rhiannon (song)")" with [Stevie Nicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Nicks "Stevie Nicks"); some critics commented Swift performed with weak vocals.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-12)[MTV News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_News "MTV News") commented the MTV Awards incident transformed Swift into a "bona-fide mainstream celebrity",[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-13) and _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ said it was refreshing to see a talented singer-songwriter like Swift "make the occasional flub".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-14) Swift began writing for her third studio album immediately after she released _Fearless_ and continued during her [Fearless Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearless_Tour "Fearless Tour") in 2009 and 2010.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15)

## Writing and lyrics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Speak_Now&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writing and lyrics")]

Because of her extensive touring schedule, Swift wrote her third album alone: "I'd get my best ideas at 3:00 a.m. in Arkansas, and I didn't have a co-writer around so I would just finish it. That would happen again in New York and then again in Boston and that would happen again in Nashville."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) Inspired by her growth into adulthood, she conceived _Speak Now_ as a loose [concept album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concept_album "Concept album") about the things she wanted to tell certain people she had met but never had a chance to.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) As with her songwriting on previous albums, Swift strove to convey emotional honesty with details as specifically as possible, believing it is important for a songwriter to do so.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) She described her songs as "diary entries" about her emotions that helped her navigate adulthood.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ew_songwriting-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-wsj_int-17) Swift chose not to follow the trend of making increasingly sexualized music by artists of her age and believed such a path would be incongruent with her artistic vision.[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-19)

Departing from _Fearless_'s theme of fairy tales and starry-eyed romance, _Speak Now_ explores introspection and reflections on broken relationships.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-LAT-20) By avoiding sexual references in its songs, the album kept Swift's "good-girl" image intact.[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-22) Some tracks were inspired by Swift's public experience, including past relationships with high-profile celebrities, which received media attention during the album's promotional rollout.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-LAT-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) The confessional lyrics of _Speak Now_ are more direct and confrontational than those on Swift's past albums.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-24) On "[Back to December](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_December "Back to December")", she asks an ex-lover to forgive her wrongdoings.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-25) Swift wrote the title track, "[Speak Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now_(song) "Speak Now (song)")", after hearing a friend's ex-boyfriend was marrying another woman; in the lyrics, the protagonist crashes the ex-boyfriend's wedding and tries to halt it.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-la_times_int-26) "[Dear John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dear_John_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Dear John (Taylor Swift song)")" narrates a devastating relationship of a 19-year-old female narrator who accuses a much-older man of manipulating her with "dark, twisted games".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) Swift's encounter with an ex-lover at an awards show, where they ignored each other despite Swift feeling a need to speak to him inspired "[The Story of Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Story_of_Us_(song) "The Story of Us (song)")".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-NYmag-27) On "[Better than Revenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Better_than_Revenge "Better than Revenge")", Swift affirms vengeance against a romantic rival who is known for "the things she does on the mattress".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-american_songwriter-28)

Romantic optimism is another theme of the album.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) The opening track "[Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mine_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Mine (Taylor Swift song)")" is about Swift's hope of attaining happiness despite her tendency to "run from love" to avoid heartbreak.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ew_songwriting-16) It was the first song she included on the track list because it represents her then-new perspective of romance.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-reuters-29) Swift had written "[Sparks Fly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparks_Fly_(song) "Sparks Fly (song)")"—a song about dangerous hints of love at first sight—before she released her 2006 debut album, [_Taylor Swift_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift_(album) "Taylor Swift (album)").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-30) She re-recorded the song for _Speak Now_ after she received fan request to release it at the 2010 [CMA Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CMA_Music_Festival "CMA Music Festival").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) "[Enchanted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enchanted_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Enchanted (Taylor Swift song)")" describes the aftermath of an encounter with a special person without knowing whether the infatuation would be reciprocated.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) "[Haunted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haunted_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Haunted (Taylor Swift song)")" is about romantic obsession and "Last Kiss" explores the lingering feelings after a breakup.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) On "[Long Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Live_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Long Live (Taylor Swift song)")", Swift expresses gratitude to her fans and bandmates.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-pitchfork-31) The lyrics of "Enchanted" and "Long Live" incorporate high-school-prom and fairy-tale imagery that recalls the youthful optimism of _Fearless_.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-RS-32)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33)

[![Image 8: Kanye West performing, wearing sunglasses](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/SXSW_2009_Kanye_West_%283378197438%29.jpg/250px-SXSW_2009_Kanye_West_%283378197438%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SXSW_2009_Kanye_West_(3378197438).jpg)

The 2009 MTV Awards incident with [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West")_(pictured)_ inspired "[Innocent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innocent_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Innocent (Taylor Swift song)")".

Besides love and romance, Swift wrote about self-perception. "[Never Grow Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never_Grow_Up "Never Grow Up")" is a contemplation of her childhood, adulthood, and future.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-american_songwriter-28)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-la_times_int-26) The self-aware "[Mean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Mean (Taylor Swift song)")", in which Swift sings about facing a man who had tried to take her down, was inspired by her detractors.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-34)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-35) Because of her confessional songwriting, the media became invested in Swift's personal life and believed each song is about a real person: an ex-lover, a friend, or an enemy.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-glamour-18)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) Although Swift was interested to hear the response from the people to whom she dedicated the songs, she did not publicly name them and believed they would realize this themselves.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-glamour-18)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) She did reveal that Kanye West, who interrupted Swift's acceptance speech at the 2009 MTV Video Music Awards, was the subject of "[Innocent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innocent_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Innocent (Taylor Swift song)")".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-NYmag-27) In the track, Swift sings about forgiving a man who wronged her; according to _[Esquire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esquire\_(magazine) "Esquire (magazine)")_, the track can be interpreted as "a simple lament of a lost love, or a former friend being forgiven".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-36)

Swift wrote as many as 40 songs and by early 2010, she had begun to select songs for the album.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-37)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-reuters-29) To ensure the album would be coherent, she played the songs to her family, friends, and the producer [Nathan Chapman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Chapman_(record_producer) "Nathan Chapman (record producer)"),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-universe-15) who had worked with Swift on both of her previous albums.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bb_release-38) Swift chose _Enchanted_ as a working title but Big Machine Records' founder [Scott Borchetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Borchetta "Scott Borchetta") recommended Swift choose a different title, deeming _Enchanted_ unfit for the album's mature perspective.[[note 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-39) She settled on the title _Speak Now_ because she thought it best captures the album's essence: "I think it's such a metaphor, that moment where it's almost too late, and you've got to either say what it is you are feeling or deal with the consequences forever... And this album seemed like the opportunity for me to speak now or forever hold my peace."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-yahoo_int-23) Swift finalized the track list by June 2010.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ew_songwriting-16)

## Composition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Speak_Now&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Composition")]

### Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Speak_Now&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production")]

Swift recorded much of _Speak Now_ with Chapman at his Pain in the Art Studio in Nashville.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40) Although _Fearless_'s commercial success allowed Swift to engage a larger group of producers, she worked solely with Chapman because she believed they had a productive relationship.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40) The recording process started with a [demo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demo_(music) "Demo (music)"); Swift recorded vocals and played guitar, and Chapman sang background vocals and played other instruments. After arranging the demos, they approached other [engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_engineer "Audio engineer") and musicians to tweak some elements, including [overdubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdub "Overdub") and [programmed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_(music) "Programming (music)") drums.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40) The first track Chapman produced with Swift on _Speak Now_ is "Mine", which they recorded within five hours.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40)

Because of his artistic autonomy, Chapman said he was responsible for "60 percent of the music on the album, including 90 percent of the guitars".[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40) Much of his production for _Speak Now_ is identical to that for _Fearless_; he programmed the drums with [Toontrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toontrack "Toontrack")'s software [Superior Drummer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superior_Drummer "Superior Drummer"), played drums on the [Roland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Corporation "Roland Corporation") Fantom G6 keyboard, added electric guitars to the arrangements, recorded Swift's vocals with an Avantone CV12 microphone and his background vocals with a [Shure SM57](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shure_SM57 "Shure SM57"), produced the [bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_(music) "Bass (music)") with an Avalon VT737 [preamplifier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preamplifier "Preamplifier"), and used Endless Audio's CLASP System to synchronize his editing on [Pro Tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_Tools "Pro Tools") and [Logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logic_Pro "Logic Pro").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40) To make the sounds align with country music stylings, Chapman worked with other Nashville musicians to replace the programmed drums with live drums and add acoustic instruments such as [fiddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiddle "Fiddle").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40) For instance, Chapman asked Steve Marcantonio to cut down programmed drums on "Mine" at [Blackbird Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackbird_Studio "Blackbird Studio") in Nashville.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40) For some tracks, including "Back to December", Swift and her team went to [Capitol Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitol_Studios "Capitol Studios") in Los Angeles to record [string orchestration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_section "String section").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-ew_songwriting-16)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-41)

After recording finished, Justin Niebank [mixed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_mixing_(recorded_music) "Audio mixing (recorded music)") the album on Pro Tools at Blackbird Studio. Within three weeks, Niebank finished mixing 17 tracks including 14 on the standard edition and three bonus tracks on the deluxe edition.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-deluxe_notes-42) Because Swift wanted _Speak Now_ to be a direct communication with her audience, Niebank infused [monoaural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoaural "Monoaural")[reverberation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverberation "Reverberation") inspired by [1950s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950s_in_music "1950s in music") and [1960s music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1960s_music "1960s music") in the mix to evoke a "vintage" and "retro" vibe that, according to Niebank, brought a sense of authenticity.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40) Hank Williams [mastered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastered "Mastered") the recordings.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40) Because much of _Speak Now_ was recorded and mixed in Nashville, Niebank believed the album stood out among popular records that were manipulated with contemporaneous technologies [Auto-Tune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auto-Tune "Auto-Tune") and [Melodyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodyne "Melodyne").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40) Although Chapman was responsible for much of the production, he said Swift's co-production credit was well-deserved: "We were really a team, very collaborative."[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-SoS-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-43)

### Music

_Speak Now_ is primarily a [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") album with radio-friendly production, as exemplified by its lead single "[Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mine_(Taylor_Swift_song) "Mine (Taylor Swift song)")".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-mcall-44)

_Speak Now_ features a [country pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_pop "Country pop") sound with prominent mainstream music elements, a style that had characterized _Taylor Swift_ and _Fearless_, and is typified by the lead single and opening track, "Mine";[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-AllMusic-45)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-mcall-44)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-American_Songwriter-46)_[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_'s James Lachno described the sound as "country bubblegum-pop".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-47) The songs' arrangements are similar to those in Swift's first two albums, but the instruments' textures are more dense and evoke strong pop and [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") influences.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTENainby2024100-48) According to the [musicologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musicologist "Musicologist") James E. Perone, the rock textures of _Speak Now_ are derived from 1970s and 1980s styles such as [new wave rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_rock "New wave rock") and [arena rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arena_rock "Arena rock").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone201729,_42-49) There were disagreements over the album's genre classification,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-EW-50) with critics categorizing it as [country rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_rock "Country rock"),[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-American_Songwriter-46)[pop rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock"),[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-bbc_music-51) and [power pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_pop "Power pop").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Now-52) The music critic [Ann Powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Powers "Ann Powers"), in a review for the _[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los\_Angeles\_Times "Los Angeles Times")_, described the album's sound as an extension of country-pop towards [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock") and bubblegum pop, with its tracks incorporating styles from "lush strings of [Céline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celine_Dion "Celine Dion")-style [kitsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitsch "Kitsch")-pop to Americana banjo to [countrypolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countrypolitan "Countrypolitan") electric guitar".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-LAT-20)

The [song structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_structure "Song structure") feature climatic build-ups, catchy pop melodies, and memorable [hooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_(music) "Hook (music)"),[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Paste-53)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33) characterized by chiming guitars, dynamic drums, and powerful choruses.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-54) The banjo-led [bluegrass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluegrass_music "Bluegrass music") track "Mean" is the only song that critics regarded as purely country music.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-billboard_best-9)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-american_songwriter-28)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-55) "Sparks Fly" has an arena-rock and pop-rock production with guitars and subtle fiddles,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-56)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202454-57) and "Speak Now" is an acoustic guitar-driven pop song with a [1950s rock chorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'50s_progression "'50s progression").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-mcall-44)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-58) "The Story of Us" and "Better than Revenge" are electric-guitar-driven [pop-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-punk "Pop-punk") songs;[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-nytimes_review-59) the former contains influences of arena rock, [dance-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance-pop "Dance-pop"), and [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"), instrumented by electric guitar riffs and subdued [mandolin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandolin "Mandolin");[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Paste-53)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Voice-60)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202463-61) "Haunted" incorporates a dramatic recurring string section.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-pitchfork-31)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-nytimes_review-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-vulture_best-63) The remaining tracks of _Speak Now_ are [ballads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_ballad "Sentimental ballad"). "Back to December" is a gentle, orchestral, string-laden [power ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-la_times_int-26)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZaleski202456-64) "Dear John" is a slow-burning, [bluesy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"), country-pop song with electric guitar [licks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lick_(music) "Lick (music)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-billboard_best-9)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Spin-65) The guitar ballad "Never Grow Up" incorporates an understated production that accompanies its wistful lyrics.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-pitchfork-31)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-mcall-44) On "Enchanted", the acoustic guitar [crescendos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crescendo "Crescendo") after each refrain and leads up to a harmony-layered [coda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coda_(music) "Coda (music)") at the end.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-pitchfork-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak_Now#cite_note-Slant-33) "Innocent" and "Last Kiss" incorporate sparse instruments;
